# Meter

> A measurement in a known range, like disk usage. It tells you which region the value's in, so your design can show it.

`<slab-meter>` · Data · built on `<meter>`

Docs: https://slab-elements.dev/components/meter/

## Import

```js
import 'slab-elements/meter.js';
```

## Usage

```html
<slab-meter label="Storage used" value="0.62"></slab-meter>
```

Screenreaders read the value as a bare number. When it means more than that, set `formatValue` to a function of `value`, such as `` (value) => `${value * 5} of 5 GB` ``, and they'll read what it returns instead.

## Elements

### `<slab-meter>`

Import `slab-elements/meter.js` to register it.

A meter with no visual styles, around a native `<meter>`: a measurement in a known range, such as disk usage, rather than progress through a task, which is Progress.

`min`, `max`, `low`, `high` and `optimum` are passed through to it, and default the way a native `<meter>`'s do. The label and the `<meter>` are both in the shadow root, so a plain `for` reference names it.

A native `<meter>` colors itself by which region its value is in, and only Firefox lets a design select that. So it's worked out here the way browsers do it, and set as `:state(optimum)`, `:state(suboptimum)` or `:state(even-less-good)`.

Screenreaders read its value as a number. Set `formatValue` to a function of `value` that says what it means, such as "3 of 5 GB", which becomes the `<meter>`'s `aria-valuetext`.

Style it through its parts and those states.

#### Attributes

| Name               | Type      | Default | Description                                                                                                      |
| ------------------ | --------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `label` (required) | `string`  |         | Names it. It's the accessible name, and the visible label where there is one.                                    |
| `hide-label`       | `boolean` | `false` | Hides the label visually and leaves it as the accessible name, for a design that shows the label some other way. |
| `high`             | `number`  |         | Where the high region starts. `max` when unset.                                                                  |
| `low`              | `number`  |         | Where the low region ends. `min` when unset.                                                                     |
| `max`              | `number`  |         | 1 when unset, as on a native `<meter>`.                                                                          |
| `min`              | `number`  |         | 0 when unset, as on a native `<meter>`.                                                                          |
| `optimum`          | `number`  |         | The best value, which decides which region is the optimum one. Halfway between `min` and `max` when unset.       |
| `value`            | `number`  | `0`     | The measurement, between `min` and `max`.                                                                        |

#### Properties

| Name          | Type                                     | Description                                                                                              |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `formatValue` | `(value: number) => string \| undefined` | What screenreaders read for the value, such as "3 of 5 GB" rather than "3". The value itself when unset. |

#### CSS parts

| Name    | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| `label` | The label   |
| `meter` | The meter   |

#### CSS states

| Name                     | Description                                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `:state(even-less-good)` | While its value is in the region furthest from the optimum one.               |
| `:state(optimum)`        | While its value is in the optimum region, as a native `<meter>` works it out. |
| `:state(suboptimum)`     | While its value is in a region next to the optimum one.                       |
